The delivery system platform focuses on the encapsulation and delivery of mRNA within cells.
The platform utilizes G0-C14, a cationic lipid that promotes endosomal escape.
PLGA is a polymer used in the platform to avoid serum nuclease degradation of mRNA.
DSPE-PEG is a lipid-PEG that stabilizes the mRNA nanoparticle system.
The nanoparticle is formed by sequentially combining mRNA with G0-C14, PLGA, and DSPE-PEG.
The nanoparticle enters an endosome in a cell and undergoes endosomal escape, leading to target mRNA translation.

IL-10@NPs nanoparticles have a uniform morphology with a size of approximately 120nm, suitable for tumor treatment and other biological applications.
Cell toxicity tests indicate that IL-10@NPs delivering IL-10-mRNA do not cause toxicity to normal cells.
IL-10@NPs can significantly inhibit tumor growth in MC-38 tumor-bearing C57 mice after tail vein injection.
IL-10@NPs can efficiently stimulate the proliferation of CD8+ T cells at the tumor site, increasing their quantity from 2.7% to 17%.
IL-10@NPs can effectively inhibit the growth of liver cancer in mice.
The delivery system allows for effective accumulation of mRNA at the site of liver tumors, as shown by in vivo fluorescence imaging.
IL-10@NPs significantly increase the IL-10 protein content at the site of liver tumors.
IL-10@NPs can effectively inhibit tumor progression and metastasis to major organs in liver cancer-bearing mice.
IL-10@NPs significantly enhance the proliferation of CD8+ T cells within liver tumors, increasing from 3.4% to 15.6%.
RT-PCR data show that IL-10@NPs enhance immune responsiveness in liver tumors by increasing the expression of granzyme, IFN-γ, TNF-α, and Fas ligand.
IL-10@NPs combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors show significant therapeutic effects, achieving complete tumor remission in 42% of mice by day 90.
Single immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment shows weak effects, while IL-10@NPs alone has limited tumor suppression.

PCR data indicates that IL-10@NPs can enhance the immune response within tumors in situ liver cancer by increasing the expression of granzyme (Gzmb), IFN-γ (Ifng), TNF-α (Tnfa), and programmed death receptor (Fasl).
Tumor immune slice results show that IL-10@NPs can increase the infiltration of CD8 cells and the expression of granzyme and IFN-γ in tumors of in situ liver cancer.
IL-10@NPs can be combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA-4) for joint treatment of mid-to-late stage in situ liver cancer.
The results indicate that the treatment effect of a single immune checkpoint inhibitor is weak, and liver cancer cells exhibit low immune responsiveness (cold tumor).
Single IL-10@NPs has a certain tumor suppression effect, but the overall effect is not satisfactory.
The combination of IL-10@NPs and immune checkpoint inhibitors can achieve significant therapeutic effects, with 42% of mice achieving complete tumor remission by day 90.
IL-10@NPs can significantly enhance the responsiveness of mice with in situ liver cancer to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

The combination of IL-10@NPs and immune checkpoint inhibitors can reverse the inhibitory effect of cold tumors on immunotherapy and significantly extend the median survival of mice from 19 days to over 90 days.
